The lemon damselfish Pomacentrus moluccensis is a common inhabitant of Indo-Pacific coral reefs, and field surveys indicate that adult females achieve a maximum recorded body mass of approximately 19.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 19.7 grams], a value consistent with the allometric relationship observed in other pomacentrids and reflecting the energetic constraints of a small-bodied, site-attached reef fish. This asymptotic wet weight is attained after a growth period during which individuals reach their ultimate standard length of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters], a dimension that places them among the smaller-bodied damselfishes of the genus. Studies of growth trajectories in this species suggest that the transition from juvenile to adult morphology involves a conspicuous allometric shift, with the onset of gonadal maturation occurring when individuals attain a standard length of about 4 centimeters [Lp = about 4 centimeters]. At this length at puberty, the corresponding wet weight of a reproductively maturing fish is approximately 1.79 grams [Wwp = approximately 1.79 grams], reflecting the onset of gonadal recrudescence and the transition from late juvenile to early adult life history. These size benchmarks have been derived from extensive underwater visual census data and from the dissection of preserved museum specimens collected across the Great Barrier Reef.

At a sustained water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], the embryonic development of Pomacentrus moluccensis proceeds rapidly, with the age at birth or hatching occurring approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days] after fertilisation. The newly emerged yolk-sac larva, still reliant on its endogenous nutrient reserves, exhibits a wet weight at birth of just 0.0029 grams [Wwb = 0.0029 grams], a minuscule mass typical of pelagic-spawning pomacentrids and reflecting the low maternal investment per offspring characteristic of this reproductive mode. This lecithotrophic larval stage is brief, and the rapid depletion of yolk reserves triggers the onset of exogenous feeding, at which point the free-swimming larva begins to actively forage on planktonic prey. The temperature dependence of these early developmental rates is marked, and this value represents the typical thermal regime of shallow reef flat environments where spawning is most frequently observed during the austral summer months.

Under identical thermal conditions of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for Pomacentrus moluccensis in the wild has been estimated at approximately 2,920 days (2920 days) [am = 2920 days], a lifespan that is notably longer than that of some congeneric species and may reflect the protective influence of wave-exposed reef habitats reducing predation risk. This estimate of natural lifespan completion is based on long-term mark-recapture studies conducted on protected reef slopes where fishing pressure is minimal. Reproductive activity begins several years prior to this upper age limit, and individuals are capable of spawning repeatedly across multiple breeding seasons. The relatively extended lifespan, considered in context with the species' moderate body size, suggests a life-history strategy that balances early reproductive investment with the maintenance of somatic condition over successive years. Senescence has not been systematically documented in this species, but field observations indicate that reproductive output may decline in the oldest age classes.

Reproductive output in Pomacentrus moluccensis was assessed during a field study on the Great Barrier Reef, where spawning activity was monitored daily. Nest-guarding males maintain territories on rubble substrata, and females deposit clutches that average 444 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 444 eggs per spawning event]. Given that individual females participate in approximately 7 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 7 spawning events per year], the annual reproductive effort is considerable for a fish of this body size. The daily reproduction rate is therefore composed of these two components, with the product of clutch size and event frequency determining total yearly fecundity. This pattern of iteroparous reproduction, with multiple discrete clutches produced annually, is typical of many tropical damselfishes and reflects the stable thermal conditions of reef environments, where a sustained water temperature of 28.6 °C [T = 28.6 °C] permits continuous gonadal recrudescence throughout much of the year.

Comparative analysis of growth and reproductive parameters across pomacentrid species reveals that Pomacentrus moluccensis exhibits a moderate pace of life relative to its congeners. Although individuals reach the standard length at puberty of 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters] within their first year, the subsequent attainment of the full adult standard length of 9 centimeters [Li = 9 centimeters] takes considerably longer, reflecting a post-pubertal growth phase that accounts for the majority of the ultimate wet weight of 19.7 grams [Wwi = 19.7 grams]. This pronounced post-maturational growth, from the 1.79 grams [Wwp = 1.79 grams] at puberty to over ten times that mass as adults, underscores the substantial energetic investment in somatic expansion following the onset of reproductive capability, a pattern that contrasts with the negligible increase from the birth mass of 0.0029 grams [Wwb = 0.0029 grams] to the size at puberty.
